text: A police‑officer may arrest a person without a warrant when the officer has reason to believe the person is liable to be arrested under any of the categories listed in section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. These include: (i) a person who commits a cognizable offence in the officer’s presence; (ii) a person against whom a reasonable complaint, credible information or reasonable suspicion exists of having committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years; (iii) a person against whom credible information shows he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of more than seven years or a death sentence; (iv) a person found in possession of an implement of house‑breaking; (v) a proclaimed offender; (vi) a person found in possession of suspected stolen property; (vii) a person who obstructs a police‑officer, escapes or attempts to escape lawful custody; (viii) a person reasonably suspected of being a deserter from the armed forces; (ix) a person involved in an act committed abroad that would be an offence in Bangladesh; (x) a released convict breaching any rule made under section 565; and (xi) a person for whose arrest a requisition has been received from another police‑officer that specifies the person and the offence. In all cases the officer must have reason to believe the person has committed the offence and must be satisfied that the arrest is necessary for investigation, prevention of further offence, preservation of evidence, or to ensure the person’s presence in court.

citations.quote: Any police-officer may, without an order from a Magistrate and without warrant, arrest- firstly, any person who commits, in the presence of a police-officer, a cognizable offence; secondly, any person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years

any person against whom credible information has been received that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to more than seven years whether with or without fine, or with death sentence
any person having in his possession without lawful excuse, the burden of proving which excuse shall lie on such person, any implement of house breaking
any person who has been proclaimed as an offender either under this Code or by order of the Government

any person in whose possession anything is found which may reasonably be suspected to be stolen property and who may reasonably be suspected of having committed an offence with reference to such thing
any person who obstructs a police-officer while in the execution of his duty, or who has escaped, or attempts to escape, from lawful custody
any person reasonably suspected of being a deserter from the armed forces of Bangladesh

any person who has been concerned in, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made or credible information has been received or a reasonable suspicion exists of his having been concerned in, any act committed at any place out of Bangladesh, which, if committed in Bangladesh, would have been punishable as an offence
any released convict committing a breach of any rule made under section 565, sub-section

any person for whose arrest a requisition, has been received from another police-officer, provided that the requisition specifies the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made

text: The police may detain a person arrested without a warrant for up to twenty‑four hours (excluding the time needed to travel to the Magistrate’s Court), unless a special order under section 167 is obtained.

citations.quote: shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 167, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.
take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police-station.

text: The search of a woman must be carried out by another woman, observing strict decency.

citations.quote: Whenever it is necessary to cause a woman to be searched, the search shall be made by another woman, with strict regard to decency.

text: Only the amount of restraint that is necessary to prevent the arrested person’s escape may be used; no more restraint than that is permitted.

citations.quote: The person arrested shall not be subjected to more restraint than is necessary to prevent his escape.

text: When making an arrest a police officer must: (a) bear a clear identification of his name; (b) disclose his identity and show his identity card if asked; (c) prepare a memorandum of arrest that is attested by a suitable witness; (d) have the memorandum countersigned or thumb‑impressed by the arrested person if he does not refuse; (e) within 24 hours inform a family member, relative or nominated friend of the arrest, giving the time, place and custody details; (f) if the arrested person has any injury, arrange for medical examination and first‑aid and obtain a medical certificate; and (g) allow the arrested person, if he wishes, to consult a lawyer of his choice or meet a close relative, preferably within twelve hours.

citations.quote: bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name which will facilitate easy identification
disclose his identity and if demanded, shall show his identity card to the person arrested and to the persons present at the time of arrest
prepare a memorandum of arrest which shall be- (i) attested by at least one witness, who is a member of the family of the person arrested or a respectable inhabitant of the locality
countersigned or thumb-impressed by the person arrested if not refused by him

intimate, where the accused is arrested from a place other than his residence, to a family member, relative, or a friend nominated by the person arrested, as soon as practicable but not later than twenty four hours

ensure, if any mark of injury is found on the body of the person arrested, the examination and first aid treatment of the person by a medical officer... obtain a certificate from the attending medical officer
(f) allow the person arrested, if he so desires, to consult a lawyer of his choice or to meet any of his nearest relation, preferably within twelve hours of such arrest

text: Yes. The Code of Criminal Procedure requires that a police officer inform the person being arrested of the reasons for the arrest at the time of the arrest.

citations.quote: Every police-officer arresting any person without warrant shall, at the time of making arrest, communicate to him the reasons for which he is arrested.

text: When information about a cognizable offence is given to the officer in charge of a police‑station, it must be reduced to writing (or written by the officer or under his direction), read back to the informant, signed by the informant, and the substance entered in a book kept by that officer in the form prescribed by the Government.

citations.quote: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence if given orally to an officer in charge of a police‑station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the Government may prescribe in this behalf.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a police officer may not investigate a non‑cognizable offence unless a Magistrate first orders the investigation.

citations.quote: No police-officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate of the first or second class having power to try such case

text: Yes. Under section 156 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an officer in charge of a police‑station may investigate a cognizable case without a Magistrate’s order.

citations.quote: Any officer in charge of a police-station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case

text: Yes. A police officer conducting an investigation may, by a written order, require a person who appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case to attend before him, and that person must comply.

citations.quote: may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself of any person ... who, ... appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case; and such person shall attend as so required.

text: No. A witness is not bound to answer questions whose answers would tend to expose him to a criminal charge, penalty or forfeiture.

citations.quote: Such person shall be bound to answer all questions relating to such case put to him by such officer, other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, a statement made to a police officer during an investigation must not be signed by the person making it.

citations.quote: No statement made by any person to a police-officer in the course of an investigation under this Chapter shall, if reduced into writing, be signed by the person making it;

text: No. A police officer is prohibited from offering any inducement, threat or promise to obtain a statement.

citations.quote: No police-officer or other person in authority shall offer or make, or cause to be offered or made, any such inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in the Evidence Act, 1872, section 24.

text: A Magistrate who is a Metropolitan Magistrate, a Magistrate of the first class, or a Magistrate of the second class specially empowered by the Government (provided he is not a police‑officer) may record a confession. Before recording it, the Magistrate must explain to the person that he is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does, the confession may be used as evidence against him.

citations.quote: Any Metropolitan Magistrate, any Magistrate of the first class] and any Magistrate of the second class specially empowered in this behalf by the Government may, if he is not a police-officer record any statement or confession
A Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so it may be used as evidence against him

text: If, after arrest, the police determine that the investigation cannot be finished within the 24‑hour period fixed by section 61, the officer in charge (or a police‑officer of at least sub‑inspector rank) must immediately send a copy of the diary entries to the nearest Judicial Magistrate and forward the accused to that Magistrate. The Magistrate may then authorize detention of the accused (in police custody) for up to fifteen days, but lower‑class magistrates cannot do so. The Magistrate can also order a medical examination of the accused before or after custody if there are signs of injury or an allegation of torture. For offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or more than ten years, the Court of Session may, at its discretion, release the accused on bail.

citations.quote: Whenever any person is arrested and detained in custody, and it appears that the investigation cannot be completed within the period of twenty-four hours ... the officer ... shall forthwith transmit ... a copy of the entries in the diary ... and shall at the same time forward the accused to such Magistrate.

The Magistrate ... may ... authorize the detention of the accused in such custody ... for a term not exceeding fifteen days in the whole; ... no Magistrate of the third class ... shall authorize detention in the custody of the police.

may order that the accused be examined by a medical officer of nearest government hospital before he is handed over to such custody; ... if ... there appears to be any mark of injury ... the Magistrate shall direct that the accused be examined by a medical officer ...

the Court of Session may, if the offence to which the investigation relates is punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment exceeding ten years, release the accused on bail to the satisfaction of such Court

text: A magistrate may take cognizance of an offence (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute the offence; (b) upon a written report of such facts made by any police‑officer; or (c) upon information received from any person other than a police‑officer, or upon his own knowledge or suspicion that the offence has been committed.

citations.quote: upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence; (b) upon a report in writing of such facts made by any police-officer; (c) upon information received from any person other than a police-officer, or upon his own knowledge or suspicion, that such offence has been committed.

text: When a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on the basis of a complaint, he must immediately examine the complainant (and any witnesses present, if he deems it necessary) and put the substance of that examination in writing, having it signed by the complainant or witness and by the Magistrate. However, if the complaint is already in writing, the Magistrate is not required to make such an examination before transferring the case.

citations.quote: A Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence on complaint shall at once examine ... and the substance of the examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed ... and also by the Magistrate
when the complaint is made in writing, nothing herein contained shall be deemed to require such examination before transferring the case under section 192

text: A Magistrate may postpone issuing process against the person complained about when, on receiving a complaint of an offence he can take cognizance of (or one transferred to him), he thinks it appropriate and records the reasons in writing. He may do so to compel the attendance of the complained‑against person and either investigate the case himself or, if he is not a third‑class Magistrate, direct an inquiry or investigation by a subordinate Magistrate, a police‑officer or any other person he deems fit. This postponement is allowed provided that, unless the complaint was made by a Court, the requirements of section 200 have been complied with, and it is also permitted where the offence appears to be triable exclusively by a Court of Session.

citations.quote: may, if he thinks fit, for reasons to be recorded in writing, postpone the issue of process for compelling the attendance of the person complained against, and either inquire into the case himself or, if he is a Magistrate other than a Magistrate of the third class, direct an inquiry or investigation to be made by any Magistrate subordinate to him, or by a police-officer, or by such other person as he thinks fit, for the purpose of ascertaining the truth of falsehood of the complaint

Provided further that where it appears to the Magistrate that the offence complained of is triable exclusively by a Court of Session, the Magistrate may postpone the issue of process for compelling the attendance of the person complained against and may make or cause to be made an inquiry or investigation as mentioned in this sub-section for the purpose of ascertaining the truth or falsehood of the complaint.

text: A magistrate may dismiss a complaint when, after considering the complainant’s statement on oath (if any) and the result of any investigation or inquiry, he judges that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding.

citations.quote: may dismiss the complaint, if ... there is in his judgment no sufficient ground for proceeding.

text: An accused must be discharged before a charge is framed if (1) the Magistrate, after examining the record and hearing the parties, finds the charge to be groundless, and (2) the Public Prosecutor withdraws the prosecution before a charge has been framed.

citations.quote: if the Magistrate ... considers the charge to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing.
if it is made before a charge has been framed, the accused shall be discharged in respect of such offence or offences;
